newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Carnival sets sail with Destiny.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Carnival sets sail with Destiny.

text.p: Bookings for the Destiny, the world's newest and biggest cruise liner, are off to "a very good start," Carnival Corp Chairman Micky Arison told Reuters.
The Destiny, the world's first cruise ship to top 100,000 tons, will make its first scheduled cruise this weekend.
"Bookings are off to a very good start," Arison said in an interview. "We're up into the 80s (percent capacity) for the entire winter season for the Destiny."

Virtually everything on the ship -- from its three-story showroom to a 214-foot water slide -- is bigger than usual. The ship has room for 3,400 passengers and crew. It is nine decks high, making it taller than the Statue of Liberty.

But the sheer size of the Italian-made ship presents logistical problems in keeping it stocked with supplies and in negotiating small harbors. In just one week at sea, the Destiny goes through 42,000 eggs, 22,000 pounds of shrimp and 33,000 bottles of beer.

"I don't think we would get involved in a much bigger ship. We've already pushed the envelope on size," Arison said. "You're building an asset that is going to be around for 30 years, and it has to be flexible to accommodate changing market tastes and changing ports of call."
The ship, which is the length of three football fields, is too wide to pass through the Panama Canal.
Carnival spent $400 million on the ship, and has $2.2 billion worth of other new ships on order.

But the ship won't remain the world's biggest for long. Princess Cruise, a unit of Peninsular & Oriental Steamship Navigation Co, is building a vessel that will edge past the Destiny in size, according to industry analysts.
The Destiny will offer seven-day Caribbean cruises from Miami, joining Carnival's other 10 ships that carry between 100 and 2000 passengers.

Arison, who said in a statement one month ago that the company was headed for record earnings this year, declined to comment on Wall Street earnings estimates. The company's fiscal year ends on November 30.

To extend its reach beyond the North American market, Carnival earlier this year signed partnership agreements with Britain's Airtours Plc and South Korea's Hyundai Corp to develop cruises in Europe and Asia.
"We've been very, very pleased with the Airtours arrangement," Arison said.
The Tropical will make its first sailing from Inchon, South Korea, in the spring of 1998. The ship may carry the Carnival name to take advantage of the popularity of western brands, he said.

"We think there is great potential with the growing middle-class market in Asia. We're prepared to add capacity if necessary and we may buy ships if we need to," he said." Although industry watchers have speculated that Carnival might be interested in a partnership with Italy's smaller Costa cruise line, Arison downplayed the rumors.
"The cruise industry will continue to consolidate," he said. "It shouldn't be a surprise that Costa is out there looking."

"We are always, constantly talking to the smaller players in the industry, and we've probably talked to just about everybody at one time or another," Arison added. "We see a lot of potential in Britain, Scandinavia, Germany and Europe. We want to play a role in that growth." -- Miami news bureau, 305-374-5013
